channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: Tutor Intelligence Raises $75 Million to Expand Robots That Warehouses Hire by the Hour
item.description: Tutor Intelligence, a robotics company spun out of MIT, announced a $75 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz, bringing its total raised to $117 million. Its two robot workers are not sold; customers pay by the hour or by the item picked, and remote human operators — the tutors in the name — guide the machines while generating the data that trains them.
item.content:encoded:
Tutor Intelligence announced a $75 million Series B on Monday, November 2, led by Andreessen Horowitz, with Union Square Ventures and Neo — the firms that led its Series A and seed rounds — also taking part. The round brings the company's total capital raised to $117 million. Tutor is based in Watertown, Massachusetts, was founded out of MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, and is led by co-founder and chief executive Josh Gruenstein, with Alon Kosowsky-Sachs as co-founder.

The company builds, manufactures and operates two robot workers, and sells their work rather than the machines. Sonny is a two-armed robot on wheels for picking individual items; Cassie is a mobile arm that moves packages between pallets and containers — at up to 18 items a minute, as described in launch coverage. Customers pay by the hour or by the pick, on month-to-month terms; the company's site prices the robots from $14 an hour, with support and model updates included, so Tutor carries the cost of a robot that stands idle. The robots are internet-connected and work in production facilities with input from remote human operators — the tutors of the company's name. Every task completed generates real-world work data, which the company uses to train its robot foundation models; a facility it opened this year evaluates robot policies across 100 physical robots.

What the round does and does not establish is stated in the company's own figures. Tutor says its robots now operate in nearly four times as many facilities as a year ago, and it projects more than 1,000 robots under contract by the end of 2027 — a projection, not a current count. Valuation, customer names and revenue are not disclosed. The test of the model is utilization: hourly pricing works for customers precisely because the idle-time risk sits with Tutor, so the business succeeds if its fleet stays busy enough, across enough sites, for the training data and the rental income to compound together.

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Tops a New Independent Test of Agent Work; the Best Score Was 12%
item.description: SemiAnalysis published GDPx on Monday, a benchmark of agent tasks drawn from valuable work domains. Claude Opus 5.5 scored highest at 12%, ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon at 10.9% — and Carbon completed its tasks at about a third of the cost. Even the leader finished roughly one task in eight.
item.content:encoded:
SemiAnalysis, the research firm, published a new benchmark on Monday, November 2: GDPx, which it describes as a frontier-level test of how well AI models perform agent tasks across the most valuable work domains. The results, reported by Gadgets360 from the firm's release, rank Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 first at 12%, Google's Gemini 4 Carbon second at 10.9%, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra third at 9.6% and Meta's Muse Wonder Full fourth at 9.0%. The firm's own framing is the sobering part: even the best model completes about one task in eight — 'even the best model scores just 12%,' in its words.

The cost table reverses part of the ranking. Gemini 4 Carbon was the most cost-efficient of the leaders at $16.29 per task, against $51.41 for Claude Opus 5.5 and $53.99 for GPT-6 Astra — roughly a third of the cost for a score about one point lower. For a buyer choosing an agent model, the two tables answer different questions: which model finishes the most hard tasks, and what each finished task costs. Edition 011 reported Carbon's launch for long-running engineering and cyber work, with access limited at first to vetted defenders; GDPx is the first independent comparison to place it against the other frontier models on general agent work.

The caveats belong with the numbers. The figures are SemiAnalysis's, from a benchmark released the same day, and this paper is reporting them through secondary coverage of the firm's release; the methodology is new and has not been run by other evaluators. A 12% score measures completion under this benchmark's setup and task selection, not general capability. What the release establishes is narrower and still useful: an independent evaluator has put the frontier's agent claims into one table, with costs attached, and the top of the table is low.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: Palantir Revenue Rises 96% to $2.31 Billion as U.S. Commercial Sales Pass Government Sales for the First Time
item.description: Palantir's third quarter beat expectations and the company raised its full-year guide, and U.S. commercial revenue passed U.S. government revenue for the first time in its history. The weaker line was new business signed: total contract value rose 6% from a year earlier, after rising 49% in the second quarter. Shares fell in after-hours trading.
item.content:encoded:
Palantir reported third-quarter results after Monday's close: revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% from a year earlier and 20% from the second quarter, against about $2.18 billion expected in the LSEG consensus cited by CNBC. Adjusted earnings per share were $0.44 against $0.41 expected. GAAP net income was $1.128 billion, a 49% margin; adjusted income from operations was $1.427 billion, a 62% margin; adjusted free cash flow was $1.216 billion. The quarter was the first in which revenue passed $2 billion.

The mix changed in a way the company has predicted for years. United States revenue was $1.937 billion, 84% of the total. Within it, commercial revenue reached $984 million, up 148% from a year earlier, and passed United States government revenue — $953 million, up 96% — for the first time in the company's history, as chief executive Alex Karp noted in the release. Net dollar retention was 165%. A company founded on government contracts now takes more United States revenue from companies than from the state.

The guide rose and the new-business line slowed; the report carried both. Palantir raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $8.530–8.534 billion, about 91% growth, from $8.150–8.158 billion, and guided the fourth quarter to $2.649–2.653 billion against about $2.46 billion expected, Reuters reported. But total contract value closed in the quarter was $2.918 billion, up 6% from a year earlier, after $3.373 billion and growth of 49% in the second quarter; United States commercial contract value rose 11%, after 153% in the second quarter, a comparison William Blair's Louie DiPalma flagged in coverage of the report. Shares had closed the regular session down 3.13% at $178.34, and most after-hours reports showed a further decline of about 3%, though at least one report had the stock higher in extended trading.

item.title: OpenAI Says Its Future U.S. Data Centers Will Cut Power Use When Local Grids Are Strained
item.description: OpenAI launched the Grid Protectors Program on Monday: campuses it develops itself will carry agreed limits on how much power they draw during grid emergencies, negotiated utility by utility. The first is a planned Georgia campus where up to 1,000 megawatts — about a third of the site's contracted supply — can be curtailed on request.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI launched the Grid Protectors Program on Monday, November 2. The program puts electricity curtailment commitments into the campuses OpenAI develops directly: each site will agree with its utility, regulators and policymakers how much demand it can reduce during grid emergencies, how quickly, and for how long. Terms will differ by location. Where local equipment allows, campuses may also supply power to the grid from on-site generation or storage. The company stated its own limit plainly: campus flexibility cannot replace investment in new energy supply and transmission.

The pilot is a contract that already exists. Project Camellia, OpenAI's planned campus in Effingham County, Georgia, is expected to need about 3,200 megawatts, delivered in phases between 2028 and 2032 under a 25-year agreement with Georgia Power that state regulators approved in August. The agreement lets the utility reduce energy delivered to the campus by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand — about a third of the site's contracted supply, and, in the company's comparison, roughly the average electricity demand of 700,000 households. OpenAI will pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs of the site and provide financial assurances intended to protect other customers.

The program answers a specific objection that has followed the buildout through this paper's record: that data centers take firm power and leave other customers with the cost of the grid built to serve them. Edition 001's lead was a grid connection refused; Edition 014 recorded a federal court letting a Clean Air Act suit over a data center's turbines proceed. A campus that can be turned down on request is a different kind of load from one that cannot. What remains unproven is scale: outside Georgia there are no other campuses, utilities or figures named yet, the Georgia campus is unbuilt, and its first power is not due until 2028.

item.title: Netflix's Ad Tier Will Be Counted in Australia's Official TV Ratings
item.description: Australia's ratings body will fold Netflix's advertising-tier viewing into the same measurement advertisers use for broadcast television. In the third quarter, Netflix held 19.7% of streaming viewing on connected TVs there — and its ad tier alone, at 5.1%, sat close to Prime Video and Disney+.
item.content:encoded:
Netflix's advertising-supported tier will be counted inside Australia's official television ratings, under an agreement between the ratings body OzTAM and Nielsen reported on November 2. The first stage is already reflected in OzTAM's third-quarter Streamscape reporting to subscribers: for the first time it separates Netflix's ad-tier and non-ad-tier viewing on connected televisions, with other devices to be added later. From February 1, 2027, ad-tier viewing at the level of individual programs will be available inside VOZ, the country's total-TV measurement system, delivered monthly.

The third-quarter shares explain why advertisers wanted the tier measured. Of streaming viewing on connected TVs in Australia, 'Other Video' held 23.4%, YouTube 23.2% and broadcaster video on demand 21.7%; Netflix held 19.7% — of which the ad tier alone was 5.1%, close to Prime Video's 6.1% and Disney+'s 6.0% for their whole services. An ad tier that can be measured in the same currency as broadcast television can be bought like television; that, rather than the viewing itself, is what changed on Monday. The figures are Australian and cover connected TVs only, and they are the ratings body's, reported by TV Blackbox.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Flexible Links Let Researchers Build Nanoparticle Crystals With New Arrangements
item.description: MIT researchers assembled nanoparticles into ordered crystals using highly flexible connector molecules, and the flexibility — not rigidity — is what let them control how many neighbors each particle binds to.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Marriott Raised Its Full-Year Hotel Revenue Forecast After a Stronger Third Quarter
item.description: Marriott's revenue per available room rose 6.5% worldwide in the third quarter — 7.4% in the United States and Canada — and the company raised its full-year growth outlook to 4.5% to 5%. Travel demand held up in most regions; Greater China was the exception, with revenue per room flat.
item.content:encoded:
Marriott International reported third-quarter results on Monday that ran ahead of the expectations it had set in August. Revenue per available room — the hotel measure that combines occupancy and the rate charged — rose 6.5% worldwide in constant dollars, and 7.4% in the United States and Canada. Adjusted earnings per share rose 22% to $3.02, beating the $2.86 consensus estimate compiled by Zacks, on revenue of $7.01 billion, up 8%. Rate did most of the work: the average daily rate rose 4.8%, while occupancy improved 1.1 percentage points to 72.5%.

The company raised its full-year 2026 outlook for worldwide revenue-per-room growth to 4.5% to 5%, from the 3% to 3.5% it had guided in August; the third quarter itself, at 6.5%, came in above the 3.5% to 4% range given for it. Greater China was the exception, with revenue per room flat, which management attributed to uneven consumer spending and major typhoons. The preliminary view for 2027, given on the earnings call, is growth of 3.5% to 4.5%. Hilton's third quarter, reported October 27, showed the same direction — comparable revenue per room up 5.8% and a raised full-year outlook — so Monday's report reads as a sector pattern rather than one company's quarter: travelers are still traveling, and hotels are charging more for the rooms.

item.title: A Common Methyl Donor Sped Liver Regeneration in Mice — and in Patients, in One Study
item.description: Researchers traced how a healing liver protects its growth proteins from disposal, then found that giving the methyl donor SAM accelerated regeneration in both mice and patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: An Enzyme in the Infant Gut Unlocks Sugars in Breast Milk That Formula Does Not Contain
item.description: Bacteria that colonize a newborn’s gut make an enzyme that frees specific sugars from breast milk — sugars carried on short protein chains, present in human milk and not in formula. The finding names one concrete way milk feeds the microbes, not only the baby.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: A small Cretaceous dinosaur, Infernogallus jamesi, had a chewing-muscle arrangement seen today only in fruit-eating parrots — evidence that some dinosaurs ate fruit, and may have carried the seeds that spread flowering plants.

item.title: A Documentary About Elizabeth Holmes Beat a Batman Villain at the Halloween Box Office
item.description: A24's 'You Can See Everything' took $10.6 million in its third weekend to edge Warner Bros.' 'Clayface' by about $200,000, in the second-lowest-grossing weekend of the year. The documentary has made $63.9 million against a reported $7 million production budget.
item.content:encoded:
The Halloween weekend at North American theaters belonged to a documentary. 'You Can See Everything,' A24's film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, took an estimated $10.6 million in its third weekend, edging Warner Bros.' 'Clayface,' which made $10.4 million in its second. The margin was about $200,000, close enough that final receipts released Monday could reverse the order, Rentrak figures reported over the weekend indicated. Total ticket sales for October 30 to November 1 were an estimated $55.7 million, down 42.1% from the previous weekend, making it the second-lowest-grossing weekend of the year; Halloween falling on Saturday drew audiences elsewhere.

The year's totals behind the quiet weekend are not weak. Domestic ticket sales have reached $8.46 billion year to date, up 20.1% from the comparable period of 2025. The documentary itself has made $63.9 million domestically against a reported production budget of $7 million. 'Clayface' has made $44.1 million against a reported budget of $44 million. Horror, the season's reliable genre, has generated an estimated $1.38 billion domestically through November 1, about $44 million short of its full-year record set in 2025. The next test of theater demand arrives this weekend, when 'The Cat in the Hat' opens in about 4,000 theaters and 'Godzilla Minus Zero' in about 2,700.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.

item.title: Pines Planted Far From Home Grow Up to Four Times Faster, and Handle Drought Better
item.description: Across 192 sites on four continents, conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere outgrew the same species at home — and stored more sugars and starches, a reserve that appears to carry them through dry spells.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: Beating Expectations No Longer Settles the AI Argument
item.description: Apple beat its quarter and guided margins down. Palantir beat its quarter and its new-contract growth slowed. Anthropic grew 47% and swung to a loss on one procurement line. Monday's results were strong and the shares fell anyway — because the question has changed from whether demand exists to what serving it costs.
item.content:encoded:
Monday's results were, by the measures the companies chose to headline, strong. Apple beat on revenue and earnings and set records in its two largest lines. Palantir beat, grew 96% and raised its full-year guide by roughly $380 million. Anthropic, in a filing rather than an earnings release, reported revenue up 47% in a quarter. All three were marked down or argued over within hours — Apple and Palantir in after-hours trading, Anthropic in the first analyses of its amendment. The pattern is worth naming precisely, because it is not a verdict on demand.

The regular session had already made the point in index form. The S&P 500 fell 0.51% to 7,541.40, its third straight decline, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.07% to 25,164.32, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.41% to 51,983.98. About 69% of the S&P 500's components rose, by MarketWatch's closing count: the indexes fell because their largest technology weights fell, with the technology sector down 2.66% for a third straight day and semiconductor shares down about 3.4%. The day's largest cross-asset move was not in technology at all — crude oil fell about 8% on hopes of a diplomatic settlement involving Iran, with West Texas Intermediate settling at $96.08 a barrel.

What investors marked in each report was the cost of the next unit of growth. In Apple's, the December-quarter margin guide: 45% to 46%, down from 47.9%, on memory costs. In Palantir's, the growth in new contracts signed: 6%, after 49%. In Anthropic's, the $5.0 billion of compute bought short-term, which converted a profitable quarter's structure into a loss. This paper's Position in Edition 011 was that the same spending produced two different companies; Edition 012 concluded that demand was proven and financing was the open question. Monday's evidence adds a third formulation: the results are now read from the guide backward. The quarter reported is treated as settled; the argument is over the terms of the next one.

The week's remaining tests are the same kind. AMD reports tonight, into a stock that fell 7.52% on Monday to $466.84 and sits nearly 30% below its recent high, against consensus of about $13.1 billion in revenue and Data Center revenue near $8.19 billion. Nvidia reports on November 17. Anthropic's roadshow in the week of November 9 will put a public price on the filing at the top of this edition. None of these tests asks whether customers want the products. Each asks what it costs to serve them, and who bears that cost — the supplier's margin, the customer's contract, or the laboratory that bought its compute late.

item.title: Apple Reports Record September-Quarter Revenue of $114.5 Billion and Guides Holiday-Quarter Margins Lower
item.description: Apple's fiscal fourth quarter beat expectations on revenue and earnings: iPhone revenue set a September-quarter record and Services revenue reached an all-time high. The December-quarter guide carries the pressure — revenue growth of 7% to 10% with gross margin of 45% to 46%, down from 47.9%, as memory costs rise. Shares fell after the report.
item.content:encoded:
Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter results on Monday, November 2, for the quarter ended September 26: revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, and diluted earnings per share of $2.10, up 14%. Both figures beat the expectations carried into the report — about $113.35 billion of revenue and $1.99 per share in the Yahoo Finance estimates cited in coverage of the results. Net income was $30.71 billion, and the quarter closed a fiscal year with record revenue of $479 billion. It was Apple's first report under chief executive John Ternus.

The product lines split. iPhone revenue reached $57.58 billion, up 17% and a September-quarter record. Services revenue reached an all-time high of $31.57 billion, and the company said paid subscriptions passed 1.5 billion. Mac revenue rose 24% to $10.79 billion, which the earnings-call summary attributed to demand for the MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro. iPad revenue fell 10% to $6.2 billion and Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 8% to $8.3 billion, both against strong launches a year earlier. Gross margin was 47.9%, including about one percentage point from tariff refunds worth $0.05 of earnings per share.

The guide is where the report tightened. For the December quarter — Apple's largest of the year — the company expects revenue growth of 7% to 10%, which would still make it the largest revenue quarter in its history, and gross margin of 45% to 46%, down from 47.9%, citing higher memory costs. One widely circulated analysis of the report put Greater China revenue at $17.54 billion against about $18.75 billion modeled, the largest single miss in its reading. Apple shares had closed Monday down 1.83% at $338.32 before the report and fell roughly a further 3% in after-hours trading. The next dated item in the story arrives Wednesday, when testing of Alibaba's Qwen models inside Apple Intelligence begins in the developer beta in China.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: Anthropic's Profit Depended on How It Bought Its Compute
item.description: Anthropic's third quarter turns on how it bought its compute. In the second quarter, with more of its capacity under long-term arrangements, the company earned $974 million in operating income. In the third, it paid $5.0 billion for compute under short-term commitments and lost $567 million, on revenue that rose 47%.
item.content:encoded: Anthropic's third quarter turns on how it bought its compute. In the second quarter, with more of its capacity under long-term arrangements, the company earned $974 million in operating income. In the third, it paid $5.0 billion for compute under short-term commitments and lost $567 million, on revenue that rose 47%. The $895 billion of commitments in the same filing is the alternative to that bill: capacity bought years ahead, at prices set in advance. Frontier margins are therefore not mainly a pricing question. They are a procurement question, and the laboratories that locked in capacity early will keep an advantage that later money cannot quickly buy.

item.title: Anthropic's Amended IPO Filing Puts Third-Quarter Revenue at $17 Billion and Commitments at $895 Billion
item.description: Anthropic filed the first amendment to its IPO prospectus on Monday, adding a third quarter the original filing did not cover. Revenue reached $17.0 billion, up 47% from the second quarter, and the company swung back to an operating loss after paying $5.0 billion for short-term compute. Its commitments for compute and infrastructure now total about $895.4 billion. The amendment still carries no share count, no price range and no listing date.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic filed Amendment No. 1 to its IPO registration statement on Monday, November 2 (SEC Form S-1/A), adding the third quarter to a prospectus that originally covered only the first half of the year. Revenue for the three months ended September 30 was $16.956 billion — about $17.0 billion — up about 47% from the second quarter's $11.555 billion and roughly twelve times the same quarter a year earlier. Revenue for the nine months reached $33.242 billion. The growth rate slowed: the second quarter had grown about 144% over the first. In absolute terms the company still added $5.4 billion of revenue in one quarter, less than the $6.8 billion it added in the second.

The quarter's cost

Compute and infrastructure cost $9.863 billion in the third quarter, 58% of revenue, up from 48% in the second quarter. The company swung to a $567 million operating loss, after $974 million of operating income in the second quarter, and attributed the loss primarily to $5.0 billion of compute bought under short-term commitments. The headline net loss was far larger and mostly not cash: $23.29 billion for the quarter, including $21.9 billion of noncash fair-value losses on convertible notes and related instruments, and $104 billion for the nine months, including $94.3 billion of such changes, CNBC reported from the filing. Cash and short-term investments stood at about $131.8 billion at September 30.

The commitments

The amendment puts the company's aggregate purchase commitments and leases at about $895.4 billion, substantially all of it for compute and infrastructure, running through 2045, with about half expected by the end of 2030. The filing also discloses developer guarantees of up to $4.7 billion. The $895.4 billion supersedes the $542–567 billion binding count this paper quoted from the original filing in Edition 008: the amendment's schedule is broader and is now the figure on record. Set against the third quarter, the commitments total roughly thirteen years of revenue at the current quarterly rate — a comparison that will move quickly if revenue keeps compounding, and that states the scale of what has been promised before the shares are priced.

A new risk, stated in the filing

The amendment also adds risk language about the company's own research process, reported by TechCrunch from the filing text. Anthropic states that its increasing use of AI systems to accelerate its own research and development may cause its models' capabilities to advance more rapidly than its ability to develop and implement safety, alignment and security measures, and that internal estimates for future models — not current ones — indicate it may imminently meet its Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.' No current model has been designated as having crossed that threshold. The filing adds that the company does not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision, and that it is considering updates to the policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development.

What the amendment does not contain is the offering itself: no share count, no price range and no deal size, so this is not the amendment that starts the roadshow. The roadshow remains reported for the week of November 9, with a mid-November listing discussed. Edition 013 recorded OpenAI's bridge round closing at a reduced size against a $1.25 trillion valuation negotiated in private, without a public Anthropic price to argue against. That comparison now has a date.

item.title: A 237-Million-Year-Old Amphibian Appears to Have Lived Its Whole Life in the Ocean
item.description: No amphibian lives in the sea today. Chemical signatures in two armored fossils found in China match seawater, not the local rock — evidence of a marine amphibian 30 kilometers from the nearest possible island.

item.title: Golden State Won the WNBA Title in Its Second Year, in the First Game 7 in Finals History
item.description: The Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 68–63 on Saturday to win the WNBA championship in the franchise's second season. Gabby Williams scored 28 of her 30 points in the second half and was named Finals MVP.
item.content:encoded:
The Golden State Valkyries won the WNBA championship on Saturday night, beating the Atlanta Dream 68–63 in Game 7 of the Finals at Chase Center — in the franchise's second year of existence. The Valkyries are the fastest expansion team in a major North American league to win a title, and the first team in the WNBA's 30-year history to win a championship without a single All-WNBA selection on its roster that season.

The game turned on one half. Gabby Williams scored 2 points in the first half and 28 in the second — the most in any half of a postseason game in league history — finishing with 30 and the Finals MVP award, including 15 consecutive Golden State points across the third and fourth quarters. Golden State trailed 30–24 at halftime, in the first Game 7 in Finals history. Owner Joe Lacob had promised a title within the team's first five years when the franchise was announced; the parade is scheduled for Wednesday in San Francisco.

item.title: The Week Every Claim Gets a Date
item.description: Apple and Palantir report tonight. Americans vote tomorrow. On Wednesday, Qwen testing begins inside Apple Intelligence in China and Moonshot's full Kimi weights fall due. Next week Anthropic takes its prospectus on the road. After a month of filings, valuations and commitments stated as intentions, the next seven days convert several of them into dated, checkable facts.
item.content:encoded:
The Tomorrow Post's October was a month of statements about the future, most of them dated in someone else's interest: a bridge round targeted at a Friday, a roadshow penciled for a November week, weights promised by a Wednesday. November's first full week is when a run of those statements meet dates that other people control.

Tonight, Apple and Palantir report after the close — the first earnings since Friday's selloff took the Nasdaq down 2.86% to its lowest close since July. Apple's consensus sits near $113 billion in revenue, and the report is its first under chief executive John Ternus, with memory costs climbing into the December-quarter guide. Palantir reports against a guide of $2.160 to $2.164 billion that consensus has already stepped over. One company tests whether consumer demand outruns a cost squeeze; the other tests whether enterprise AI spending shows up as revenue at the rate its valuation assumes.

Tomorrow, the test is electoral. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are decided, and the prediction markets covered in this edition settle a $1.4 billion claim to forecast the result. AMD reports the same evening. On Wednesday the tests turn technical: developers in China begin testing Qwen inside Apple Intelligence, and Moonshot's full Kimi K3.1 Pro weights fall due — a promise made on October 23, when the company also said it had removed cyber data from the open weights. Whether the released weights match the described model is checkable within days by anyone who downloads them.

None of these dates was set by the companies being tested, which is what distinguishes the week. A roadshow can slip and a round can be resized — October showed both. An election, an earnings calendar, a promised file and a regulator's deadline cannot be resized by their subjects. By Friday's jobs report, and certainly by Anthropic's roadshow in the week of November 9, several of the numbers this paper has carried as intentions will have become results, and the dossiers will record which ones survived contact with their dates.

item.title: Prediction Markets Have Traded More Than $1.4 Billion on the Midterms, One Day Before the Vote
item.description: Trading on 2026 midterm markets passed $1.4 billion in CNN's analysis — nearly $1.1 billion of it on Kalshi and more than $340 million on Polymarket. Tuesday's vote is the first full test of the platforms' claim to forecast elections, and of the regulators who have pledged to police insider trading on them.
item.content:encoded:
More than $1.4 billion has been traded on prediction markets about the 2026 midterm elections, according to a CNN analysis of the platforms' public data — nearly $1.1 billion of it on Kalshi, the largest United States operator, and more than $340 million on Polymarket across its United States and offshore platforms. ForecastEx, owned by Interactive Brokers, accounts for more than $6.4 million. The figures measure trading volume — the value of contracts changing hands before markets close — not the sum originally wagered.

The structure of the trading matters more than the total. A nonprofit tracker, the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, counted 21,811 individual congressional markets across the platforms by September 30, with only about 16% of them on who wins a race; the majority trade on margins of victory, and more than $20 million had traded on outcomes that can be known in advance, such as candidate withdrawals and endorsements. Kalshi has suspended at least six 2026 candidates for betting on their own races, CNN reported, and federal regulators have pledged to act on insider trading around the midterms.

Tuesday is the settlement date for the cycle's central claim. Kalshi's chief executive, Tarek Mansour, has described the midterms as a test of market-based forecasting, and Polymarket cites a 98% accuracy rate for its election markets one day before an election — a company figure, carried here as the company's claim. Edition 013 reported Kalshi's $1 billion Series G at a $40 billion valuation and its stated share of the prediction market; what Tuesday adds is a public score. If the markets call the close races well, they enter the next cycle as a forecasting source news organizations cite alongside polls. If they miss, the $1.4 billion reads differently — as volume in search of a result.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: OpenAI Will Train on Daybreak Blue Cybersecurity Sessions From November 29, Sessions Previously Excluded From Training
item.description: OpenAI told members of its Trusted Access for Cyber program that session data from Daybreak Blue, its defensive-security tier, will be used for model training from November 29. Those sessions were previously excluded from training even for users who had switched training off. After members objected, the company promised a separate opt-out whose mechanics it has not described.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI will use session data from Daybreak Blue — the defensive tier of its Trusted Access for Cyber program — to train its models starting November 29, The Decoder reported on October 31, from an email the company sent to program members. Daybreak gives approved security researchers access to models for defensive work such as vulnerability triage, secure code review and incident response. Until this change, Daybreak Blue sessions were excluded from training altogether, including for members who had turned off the general 'improve the model for everyone' setting.

The follow-up reporting on November 1 adds a second source: OpenAI's updated public data-controls page now states that content from Daybreak Blue sessions on personal accounts may be used to improve its models even when that setting is off. The company says the training use is intended to strengthen safeguards against cyber misuse, and that interactions flagged during safety reviews may be used for safety purposes. Activity outside Trusted Access sessions continues to follow the user's setting, and inputs from Business, Enterprise, Edu and API services are not used for training by default.

The response from members was immediate. Security researcher Sean Heelan, in a post cited in the coverage, argued the change takes researchers' private work — sessions that can contain vulnerability details, exploit proofs and client system layouts — and predicted it would reduce use of the program. OpenAI then sent a second email promising a separate opt-out for Daybreak sessions. Neither the emails as reported nor the public page describes how that opt-out will work, what its default will be, or whether it applies to past sessions. The date that governs is November 29: unless the separate control has arrived by then, the default changes on that day.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: McDonald's Traffic Fell in the Third Quarter, and Its MONOPOLY Relaunch Produced Its Busiest Weeks of 2026
item.description: Visits to McDonald's fell 4.6% year over year in the third quarter, Placer.ai reports. In October, the return of the MONOPOLY game and Halloween Boo Buckets lifted traffic above the year's weekly average for three straight weeks, without passing the same weeks of 2025.
item.content:encoded:
McDonald's third-quarter traffic fell, and its October promotions worked — both facts arrive in the same report, three days before the company reports earnings. Placer.ai's analysis, published Monday, puts visits down 4.6% year over year in the third quarter and same-store visits down 5.1%, with traffic below the prior year in every month from March through September as higher gasoline prices weighed on household budgets.

October reversed the pattern, on promotions rather than price cuts to the core menu. The relaunch of the MONOPOLY game on October 6 and Disney villain-themed Boo Buckets on October 20 produced the chain's busiest weeks of 2026: traffic ran 2.2% above the year's weekly average in the launch week, 5.4% the next, and 7.2% the week after. The visits still did not exceed the same weeks of 2025, when both promotions also ran. McDonald's reports its third quarter before the open on Wednesday, November 4, and has signaled United States comparable sales likely slipped — which makes Wednesday's question specific: whether a game board and a Halloween bucket moved guest counts enough to change the quarter's story.

item.title: Marble Cognition Raised $3.75 Million for Agent Workers That Learn by Watching Employees Work
item.description: The Munich startup, launched today, records how employees use their tools — screenshots, clicks and keystrokes — and converts the record into a structured process map its agents can execute. The $3.75 million pre-seed was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp. Every figure about what the system captures is the company's; no customer is named in the launch coverage.
item.content:encoded:
Marble Cognition, a Munich startup, launched today with a $3.75 million pre-seed round led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, with angel investors including executives from McKinsey and Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog, SiliconANGLE reported. Marble was co-founded by German AI engineers Felix Rösner and Christophe Schmit. Its premise is that enterprise agents are now widely available, and what companies lack is a record of how their own work is actually done.

The product records work at the source. A desktop application observes employees using their tools and processes — taking screenshots and capturing clicks and keystrokes — and transforms that record into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, in the company's description, similar to code. The agents Marble calls its workers are then meant to run the mapped processes.

The company's account leaves the load-bearing questions open. No customer is named in the launch coverage, no accuracy or completion figures are published, and the monitoring at the center of the product — continuous screenshots and keystroke capture of employees — raises consent and works-council questions in its home market that the coverage does not address. What the round establishes is narrower: investors are funding the observation layer beneath enterprise agents, on the theory that the scarce input is not the agent but a faithful map of the work. That is the same scarcity GenRobot sells into for physical work, recorded in this edition — one in factories, one in offices.

item.title: A Common Methyl Donor Sped Liver Regeneration in Mice — and in Patients, in One Study
item.description: Researchers traced how a healing liver protects its growth proteins from disposal, then found that giving the methyl donor SAM accelerated regeneration in both mice and patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: GenRobot AI Raised $100 Million to Collect the Human Demonstrations Robots Learn From
item.description: The Beijing company sells the recording systems and software that capture people performing tasks — vision, hand and body movement — and turn the recordings into labeled training data for robots. Its $100 million Series A+ round was disclosed on November 2; the company says it closed in the third quarter. SAIC Motor and Baidu are among the investors named in the disclosure.
item.content:encoded:
GenRobot AI, a Beijing company that builds data infrastructure for robot developers, has completed a $100 million Series A+ round, in a financing disclosed on November 2 that the company says closed in the third quarter. GenRobot does not build robots. It builds the equipment and software used to collect human demonstrations — recordings of people carrying out tasks, capturing vision together with hand and body movement — and its Matrix platform synchronizes, cleans and labels those recordings so robot developers can train on them.

The investor list in the disclosure is broad: SAIC Motor, Baidu, Shoucheng Holdings and Galaxy General Robotics among industrial and strategic names, alongside GL Ventures, CITIC Goldstone, CCB International and Huatai Zijin among financial investors. The terms that would show how the company is valued — price, structure, and any customer or revenue figures — are not in the disclosure, which comes from a single trade report of the company's announcement; this paper has not independently verified the round's terms.

The business exists because of where the bottleneck in physical AI currently sits. A language model trains on text that already exists; a robot model trains on demonstrations that someone has to perform, record and label, task by task. Edition 014's Bleu Robotics made the adjacent bet from the software side — fewer demonstrations per task. GenRobot makes it from the supply side: demonstrations as a produced input, sold to every developer who needs them. Which side of that market keeps the value depends on how scarce clean demonstration data remains once the first generation of robots is deployed and generating its own.

item.title: Four AI Companies Will Honor One robots.txt Signal for Opting Out of AI Training
item.description: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic have each said they will honor a single shared signal in a website's robots.txt file that keeps its content out of generative AI training. One rule would replace the separate block each company requires today. Support arrives on different schedules, running into 2027, and the signal is a statement of preference, not a license.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic have each said they will honor one shared signal that lets a website keep its content out of generative AI training, The Verge reported on October 30. The signal lives in robots.txt, the file sites already use to address crawlers. A site adds a group headed by a new policy token, __usage_ai-training, and lists the paths it does not want used for training — the whole site, or everything except, in the draft's own example, a press kit. Today a publisher who wants to refuse training must write and maintain a separate block for each company's crawler.

A draft, not yet a standard

The text is an individual Internet-Draft at the Internet Engineering Task Force, written by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, and published on October 30. The IETF has not endorsed it; it has no formal standing in the standards process, and it expires on May 3, 2027 unless advanced. The draft is explicit about its limits: it states a preference about how content is used. It does not block crawling, it does not affect search indexing, and it applies to future training — it cannot withdraw content already collected.

Four schedules

Support arrives at four speeds. Anthropic says it has already begun implementing the signal, as a complement to its existing crawler controls rather than a replacement. OpenAI says it aims to implement it in the coming months, and that its existing controls, including the GPTBot block, remain in force meanwhile. Microsoft will honor the new preferences from February 1, 2027, and will stop recognizing the older tags it used for training preferences after March 1, 2027; Microsoft states that the preferences do not establish licensing or payment arrangements. Google aims to support the signal in 2027: John Mueller, its search advocate, wrote that a site which opts out with the shared token and does not mention Google-Extended will be treated as having blocked Google-Extended, the token that governs Gemini training. Meta's communications head, Andy Stone, voiced support for a common signal, The Verge reported, without saying Meta would honor this one.

What changed on October 30 is therefore narrower than the headline version of the story, and more durable. No publisher gained a new legal right, and no crawler changed its behavior that day. What publishers gained is a single line that four competing laboratories have publicly committed to read — which converts a private configuration chore into a public commitment that can be checked, company by company, against the schedules each one published.
